item.title: 10 Greatest NES Games Of All Time, Officially Ranked
item.description:
Although perhaps not as beloved as the 16-bit hardware that followed, the Nintendo Entertainment System is the most important console of all time, one that not only helped save the industry after the 1983 crash but also produced games that codified most genres. The best NES games are masterpieces that used the limitations of their era to innovate and entertain, and some of them still stand the test of time.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

To be honest, I don't generally enjoy writing these types of definitive lists, as there are just too many brilliant games to fit in one article. However, after spending the last few months revisiting the NES's catalog, I believe it is time to ask the age-old question: what's the greatest NES game ever?

While not the determining factor behind the rankings, I want to focus on games that are still playable and enjoyable today. I don't see the point of filling this type of article with games that cannot be recommended. Metroid , Kid Icarus , Dragon Quest 3 , and Final Fantasy are all landmark releases, but there's almost no reason to play them in 2026.

10 The Legend of Zelda Paved The Way To So Many 10/10 Masterpieces

Hasn't Aged Amazingly, But Its Footprint Is Huge

  • Developer: Nintendo
  • Release Year: 1986

OK, let's kick things off with a title that comes painfully close to defying the one rule I set for this article. The Legend of Zelda has not survived the aging process quite as well as the other games in this article, and I advise that younger players looking to experience the franchise's early days start with the SNES's A Link to the Past instead. However, Nintendo's classic hit too many historical milestones to ignore .

LoZ wrote the blueprint for non-linear exploration by dropping players into a sandbox and challenging them to find their own route. The dungeons were light-years ahead of the competition, as they had complex (for the time) maps that turned each one into an extensive puzzle. Yes, the game is a bit too cryptic for its own good, and it isn't particularly great on a blind playthrough, but that doesn't take anything away from what Nintendo accomplished in 1986.

9 Vice: Project Doom Oozes B-Movie Cool

An Underappreciated NES Masterpiece

  • Developer: Aicom
  • Release Year: 1991

Oh, that's right, the greatest NES games don't consist of just Nintendo releases, as the console had plenty of champions that contributed to the cause. Due to launching late in the system's life, Vice: Project Doom didn't garner all that much attention during its original run, and its legacy is that of a cult classic, at best. Fortunately, this late release came with the benefit of experience, as developers knew how to get the most out of the NES by the early '90s.

Vice: Project Doom blends three gameplay styles: side-scrolling action-platforming, driving stages with light bullet hell elements, and overhead shooter segments, all of which are executed surprisingly well. Beyond the varied gameplay, the game oozes '80s action movie cheese in the best possible way, and everything combines to create one of the most consistently gripping campaigns on the NES .

8 Legendary SNES Games That Are 100% Unplayable Now

Don’t dust off your Super Nintendo for these legendary SNES titles. They may be iconic, but they are a struggle to get through today.

By Evan Regan

8 River City Ransom Is Way More Than Just A Beat 'Em Up

An Ambitious Genre-Blender That Still Plays Like A Dream

  • Developer: Technos Japan
  • Year: 1989

If I judged these games solely on how much I enjoy playing them nowadays, River City Ransom would rank far, far higher. Although primarily seen as a beat 'em up, Technos effectively created one of the first true action RPGs , and you could easily draw a line from River City Ransom to Like a Dragon .

In an age dominated by traditional beat 'em ups, this game defied expectations by introducing free exploration, non-linear progression, RPG stats upgraded by buying food and drinks, and buyable attacks. River City Ransom took plenty of huge swings for the '80s, and pretty much everything paid off.

7 Crystalis Is The Best RPG On The NES

The NES Game That Built On The Legend Of Zelda's Foundation

  • Developer: SNK
  • Year: 1990

To be honest, NES RPGs have collectively aged like milk, and there's basically no reason to play any of them when the SNES has roughly a billion better examples of the genre's early days. The one exception is Crystalis , which took many of LoZ 's ideas and implemented them in a more well-defined world and narrative, along with introducing a more complex combat system.

Crystalis really does feel like a SNES-era action RPG that just happens to be on the NES . You have a proper magic system that lets you use utility spells like Teleport, easy-to-follow navigation that makes good use of NPCs, elemental attacks, and a sci-fi fantasy post-apocalyptic story with plenty of personality and even some nuance.

6 Castlevania 3: Dracula's Curse Is Konami At Its Early Creative Best

Style, Substance, And Companions

  • Developer: Konami
  • Year: 1989

The first true signs of the Metroidvania genre began to form in 1989. After dropping the ball with Simon's Quest , Konami went back to the challenging action-platforming of the original game, albeit with far more emphasis on non-linear paths and player choice. Castlevania 3: Dracula's Curse is a gothic horror masterclass that oozes ambiance from pretty much every single frame, and the visuals still look good today, as long as you go in with realistic expectations.

Famously, Castlevania 3 includes the inspired companion system , which lets you take another character along with Trevor Belmont. These three playable characters need to be unlocked and have wildly different movesets, which expands the campaign's replayability exponentially. None of that would matter if the gameplay wasn't rock-solid, and Castlevania 3 nails what it's trying to be: a deliberate, consequence-laden action game.

The Main Castlevania Timeline, Explained (In Chronological Order)

Castlevania features an expansive, extremely confusing timeline, and we're here to sort through it and make sense of Konami's crazy story.

By Melody MacReady

5 Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! Is Still A Complete Knockout

Nintendo Really Nailed The Formula Here

  • Developer: Nintendo
  • Year: 1987

99% of the NES's sports games are excruciating to play nowadays... thankfully, Punch-Out!! isn't a sports title. Obviously, players step into a boxing ring and trade blows with a series of opponents, but that's just the premise and not the actual gameplay feel. No, Punch-Out!! is a rhythm game , and a darn fine one at that.

Arguably the best aged NES game, Punch-Out!! utilizes a simple combat loop: block, dodge, and counter. That's pretty much all you do, but each new opponent introduces new moves, routines, and pacing, while also decreasing the margin of error. It creates this intense loop where you are always pushing past your perceived limits.

4 ​​​​​​​Contra Hit The Bullseye On Its First Go

That Time The NES Outdid The Arcade Cabinet

  • Developer: Konami
  • Year: 1987

While Castlevania 3 is Konami's most impressive NES project, Contra is the publisher's best release. A rare example of a console port being better than the arcade original, Contra nailed the run-and-gun formula right out of the gate , and only a handful of games since then have come close to replicating its magic. As long as they don't mind a few dozen deaths, anybody can pick up this classic today and have just as much fun as they would have had in the late '80s.

With responsive controls, eight-way aiming, and a weapon system that significantly changes the "gun" part of the gameplay loop, Contra was built on an absurdly strong foundation, one that only needed mediocre level design and enemies to be excellent. As it so happens, Contra also excels in those areas.

Also, Contra and the Konami Code go hand-in-hand.

3 Kirby's Adventure Is The Final NES Masterpiece

The True Birth Of A Pink Legend

  • Developer: HAL Laboratory
  • Year: 1993

HAL waited until the NES's twilight years to bring the adorable puffball to home screens, a choice that apparently was the correct one. Kirby's Adventure is the most technically immaculate game on the NES, and it pushed the console in directions that were deemed impossible at the time. It's arguably the console's only title that could actually pass for a SNES release .

We can praise the technical side of things until the end of days, but Kirby's Adventure 's "classic" status comes down to its mechanics, charm, colorful visuals, and the protagonist himself. While the series started with Kirby's Dream Land on the Game Boy, this NES game gave Kirby his copy ability, allowing him to swallow enemies and transform into a version of them.

5 Classic NES Games That Hold Up As 10/10 Masterpieces

Most NES games are easy to appreciate but hard to love, but these masterpeices have stood the test of time so well that they still feel perfect.

13
By Mark Sammut

2 ​​​​​​​Mega Man 2 Is A Proper Golden-Age Classic

Capcom Learns From The Past And Secures The Future

  • Developer: Capcom
  • Year: 1988

Frankly, the entire Mega Man series deserves to rank in this article, as Capcom dropped 5 near-masterpieces on the NES. Ultimately, Mega Man 2 deserves to be mentioned above the others, solely for the fact that it saved the Blue Bomber from an early demise after the disappointing first game. The sequel eradicated most of its predecessor's issues by vastly improving Mega Man's responsiveness and predictability, while also improving the rock-paper-scissors boss weapon system.

While I could see an argument for any of the sequel games being better, Mega Man 2 is the quintessential 8-bit action-platformer . Except for a couple of brief (and frustrating) low points, the campaign maintains its momentum for basically its entire run, and its boss roster is tough to beat. Also, the Metal Blade is one of the most OP weapons on the NES, and that's a positive.

1 ​​​​​​​Super Mario Bros. 3 Is The Greatest NES Game Ever

There's No Beating The Plumber

  • Developer: Nintendo
  • Year: 1988

I don't consider myself a contrarian, but I try to avoid going with the obvious pick if I can help it. In this case, I have no choice, as Super Mario Bros. 3 is far and away the best game on the NES.

Although naturally not the first of its kind, Nintendo pretty much defined what it means to create a timeless platformer with this sequel, and every 2D side-scroller that followed owes a debt to this legend . While everyone should experience all the games in this article, SMB3 is the only true must-play. Unlike so many foundational games that eventually succumb to their genre's harsh progress, SMB3 's snappy momentum and precision would allow it to exist alongside modern indie darlings without any issue what so ever.

item.title: How to Get Classified Weapon Camo in COD Warzone
item.description:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 's Season 1 update brings players a whole host of new content, from new Multiplayer maps to the arrival of XO1 in DMZ. Warzone also receives plenty of new additions, including the Zodiac Resurgence map and the Hajin Battle Royale map. That's not all, as Warzone players can also unlock a free Classified Weapon Camo. Here's how.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
All Season 1 Weapons in COD Modern Warfare 4 (& How to Unlock Them)

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 brings new weapons for the Season 1 update that MP, DMZ, and Warzone players can grind to unlock. Here's how.

By Nathan Round

There appears to be an issue with the challenge for the Classified Weapon Camo. During my games, although I managed to get enough kills using a Classified Weapon, the challenges progress has not tracked. I will update this guide once a fix has been issued.

How to Get the Classified Weapon Camo in COD Warzone

Classified Weapon Location in COD Warzone

To unlock the Classified Weapon Camo in Warzone and Modern Warfare 4 , you will need to get a total of 10 kills with a Classified Weapon. Those who played during the Black Ops 7 era may already be familiar with these particular guns, as they function pretty much the same way.

Getting your hands on a Classified Weapon comes down to luck, as only one will spawn the map as part of a random event, and even then it is not guaranteed. So far, I've had the most success finding them in Resurgence, but they can potentially spawn in Battle Royale, too. When a Classified Weapon drops onto the map, an alert will appear on your HUD , along with the location of a Supply Drop marked on both your map and HUD.

Simply be the first to reach and open the Supply Drop to obtain a random weapon with eight attachments. Alternatively, if another player gets there first, eliminate them and pick up the weapon from their body. From there, all you need to do is get 10 eliminations with the Classified Weapon. The challenge is cumulative, so you don't need to get all 10 kills in a single match.

By far the easiest way to complete this challenge is to jump into Resurgence Casuals. This gives you far fewer players to contend with when hunting for the Classified Weapon, while also allowing you to farm eliminations against easier opponents. Once you've secured 10 eliminations, either in a single match or across multiple games, the Classified Weapon Camo will unlock for all Modern Warfare 4 weapons.

item.title: Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave Faces an Old Three Houses Dilemma
item.description:
Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave made quite the splash on its arrival, quickly becoming the latest in a string of commercial and critical successes for Nintendo's flagship strategy series. It came as no surprise then, when sweeping plans for three waves of DLC were announced to be on the horizon. Whether this DLC will live up to Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave remains to be seen.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

There are a few hurdles developers will have to clear if they want to continue their recent hot streak. Players have been left almost entirely in the dark about what the Fortune's Weave Expansion Pass will entail, so one can only speculate about the brass tacks of it all. However, the general outline we have given should raise some concerns about the nature of following up a route-based RPG like Fortune's Weave .

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave DLC Has a Chance to Fix Its Biggest Omission

Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave's 2027 DLC could finally give four overlooked characters the spotlight the base game never did.

By Amber Warnock-Estrada

From Fates to Three Houses, Fire Emblem Has a Rocky History with DLC

Perhaps the most obvious hurdle in front of developers is simply that they have their work cut out for them. Following up on the good will established by Fortune's Weave will be difficult enough, but the DLC faces the far more intimidating challenge of adding to a game that is already ridiculous in scale. Fortune's Weave features four different routes with complete stories in their own right. This has already been overwhelming for some players to keep up with, and adding to the stack runs the risk of drowning them out entirely.

In contrast to the structure of previous Fire Emblem games like Three Houses or even Fates , Fortune's Weave allows players to take on every route semi-simultaneously during a single playthrough. There is still a level of player choice between these routes, and the order in which you tackle them matters more than one might think. When adding new stories to a game that already has a branching narrative, you run the risk of cheapening the choices that defined a player's original journey.

When adding new stories to a game that already has a branching narrative, you run the risk of cheapening the choices that defined a player's original journey.

This is certainly a pitfall Fire Emblem: Fates fell headfirst into. Whether players chose Conquest or Birthright , it all came out in the wash when Revelations was released as the definitive experience uniting both factions of the game's conflict. Players were forced to ask why they should fight and die for one side or another when they could go their own route and make everyone happy. One version rendered both of its predecessors completely irrelevant.

By the time Three Houses rolled around, developers seemed to have learned a few valuable lessons. item.title: GTA 6's Greatest Opportunity Lies Beyond the Streets of Vice City
item.description:
Rockstar’s latest Grand Theft Auto 6 gallery was officially released on November 5, 2026. It features 39 screenshots showcasing Vice City, as well as some other parts of Leonida ahead of the title’s November 19 launch. Obviously, Vice City is getting a lot of attention as usual, which makes sense considering its beautiful beaches, neon lights, and flamboyant vibe. After all, it is already one of the most recognizable locations in the entire franchise.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

However, we are already well aware of the fact that GTA 6 will be a lot more than its headline city. Rockstar’s official materials have given us yet another reason to believe that the rest of Leonida will probably have just as much to offer as the main city. From smaller communities to huge natural landscapes, it appears that the state will feature an insane amount of variety. This is a huge opportunity for Rockstar Games to fully showcase its world-building potential and show players that there are just as many adventures awaiting outside of Vice City’s busy streets.

Rockstar Officially Comments on GTA 6's Open World

Rockstar officially comments on how it expects, or hopes, players to play in GTA 6's open world.

1
By Joshua Duckworth

Leonida's Smaller Communities Could Be GTA 6's Biggest Strength

gta 6 trailer

Many players would agree that Leonida’s many smaller communities might actually turn out to be more interesting than it initially seems. So far, it appears that the idea is for every location to have its own distinct identity instead of simply existing as an extension of Vice City. To be fair, this is quite an ambitious task, but knowing what Rockstar Games is capable of, combined with the 13 years of waiting for the release of GTA 6 , there is actually a huge possibility that we will be seeing one of the most successfully developed and immersive open worlds in the industry so far. According to the studio’s official descriptions, there’s a lot more to these places than their appearances, as each one has its own local culture and social environment.

Find the odd one out before the timer hits zero.

Round 1

Which one doesn't belong?

0 / 10
10.0 s

Results

0/5

Best: 0/5

—

More Games

This is a fantastic opportunity to make every location in the game memorable and authentic as well. The studio wouldn’t even have to make all areas huge and filled with impressive landmarks as most other open-world games try to do; sometimes the people who live there, their values, and way of communicating are the qualities that can make a certain place feel truly special. So, if Rockstar Games manages to play its cards right, even smaller towns could leave a lasting impression that rivals Vice City. Of course, it’s important to remember that Leonida is not just about its cities and towns, as Rockstar has also showcased several natural environments that look completely different from the usual setting in Vice City.

Vice City could remain the game’s most recognizable destination without necessarily becoming its most memorable one.

To give an example, the Grassrives introduce an expansive swamp landscape, while Mount Kalaga National Park is all about its rugged wilderness setting. There is also the Leonida Keys area, which brings a beautiful coastal scenery into the mix. Overall, locations like these could be yet another opportunity for exciting exploration, because if one is constantly surrounded by traffic, the world will quickly start losing not only its resemblance to reality but also the excitement it brings. And even though no specific wildlife interactions have been confirmed when it comes to Leonida’s wilderness, it is definitely a thrilling possibility.

In general, many would agree that there is just something about getting into a vehicle and just driving through a game’s open world without a specific direction. Obviously, there will be plenty of opportunities for players to do so in Grand Theft Auto 6 , but the point is that this time people will be able to drive through so many different locations and cultures that, eventually, they will have immersed themselves in a world just as diverse as the one outside. This is also an opportunity to make the world feel like one enormous, connected place instead of a collection of separate destinations with nothing between them.

GTA 6's Greatest Opportunity Goes Beyond Vice City

Perhaps the strongest indication that Leonida will be more than just a pretty backdrop is that Rockstar has already confirmed that GTA 6 's protagonists Jason and Lucia will become entangled in a criminal conspiracy that stretches across the entire state. This means that even the story itself might require developers to really put effort into locations other than Vice City. Of course, this depends largely on how successfully Rockstar Games will execute its ideas and whether people’s expectations are realistic in general, but it’s safe to say that the screenshots have at least established how visually diverse the state is.

Rockstar Issues New Official Statement on GTA 6 Physical Edition
GTA 6's Greatest Opportunity Lies Beyond the Streets of Vice City
Is Kodak Black in GTA 6?
GTA 6 Gets Its First Official Black Friday Discount

If the different locations manage to contribute something meaningful to the adventure as well as the general feeling of the world, then Vice City could remain the game’s most recognizable destination without necessarily becoming its most memorable one. It would also be interesting to see if any of these areas will end up becoming fan favorites too, despite receiving less attention before launch.

item.title: New Steam Game Is Basically Zelda Meets Toy Story With a Dark Twist
item.description:
I didn't think it was possible, but I managed to pry myself free from the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remakes clutches long enough to play something different, and I'm actually glad I did. I've just stumbled on one of the most promising Zelda -likes I've played this year, though if you're expecting something colorful, adventurous, and expansive, you won't find it here. Even so, Lelu is one of those games that I think every fan of Zelda should keep an eye on, because not only is it very clearly inspired by Nintendo's flagship franchise, it has something unique to offer that sets it apart just enough. And if you want to, you can even give it a try right now with its free Steam demo, which I recently spent just over a glorious half hour with.

Add GameRant on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Lelu follows a small clockwork toy that has somehow gained consciousness and decided it wants nothing more than to escape the factory it calls home. Unfortunately, that's easier said than done, as the factory is essentially one enormous labyrinth filled with dangerous machinery and traps set by its eccentric guardian, not to mention other toys that aren't particularly interested in letting Lelu leave. Along the way, players will acquire new tools and abilities that allow them to overcome obstacles and reach previously inaccessible areas, all while solving puzzles and fighting everything from hostile toys to enormous mechanical bosses. It provides a pretty interesting Toy Story -esque premise for a Zelda -like, especially considering that the entire adventure takes place in a monochromatic toy factory rather than the sort of colorful fantasy world fans of Nintendo's franchise are probably accustomed to. But if it already sounds like something up your alley, you'll be pleased to know that it's currently slated for a January 21, 2027 release on Steam, which is only a couple of months away now.

New Steam Action RPG Is Like an N64 Zelda Soulslike, and That's Enough

Mouseward feels like an N64 Zelda game reimagined as a soulslike, and its simple combat and rewarding exploration are already more than enough for me.

By Josh Cotts

Lelu Turns Zelda Into a Monochromatic Toy Story

Check Out Lelu's Demo on Steam

Anytime I boot up a Zelda -like, I never know whether to expect a straight-up Zelda clone or something that just borrows from Zelda here and there. When it comes to Lelu , I'm actually not sure which one it is, because it literally has Cuckoos. Okay, they're not Cuccos, but it's clearly intended to be the same thing. They're actually toy chickens rather than real chickens, but there's even a side quest in Lelu 's demo where an NPC named Clocky tasks you with finding all of his missing Cuckoos in exchange for a reward. For the uninitiated, that's quite literally the premise of one of The Legend of Zelda 's most famous recurring side quests.

Wishlist Today

But enough about how Lelu compares to Zelda , let's get into how it compares to Zelda (see what I did there?). Everything in Lelu is actually fairly straightforward if you're a Zelda fan, and should you play it, you'll probably pick it up pretty quickly. There are plenty of puzzles to solve, you get a wrench that you can swing at enemies just like Link does his sword, there are hidden paths leading to secrets in its dungeon-like toy factory, and there are abilities you can unlock as you progress through the game. And despite it taking a little more thought than Zelda 's earliest hours typically do, it's not difficult by any means—at least, according to what I played in the demo.

I did die a few times during the demo, it's worth mentioning. Many of the combat arenas don't give you much space to work with, which can really complicate things when there are several enemies closing in on you. At first, things aren't that complex, but once you unlock the ability to dash, the enemies become more aggressive and throw attacks at you that will punish you for sitting still. By the end of the demo, I had to be quite a bit more thoughtful about my next move than I did when I started. It's tense, but it's a fun kind of tension. At the very least, the incredible soundtrack helps with those more intense moments.

Lelu is one of those games that I think every fan of Zelda should keep an eye on, because not only is it very clearly inspired by Nintendo's flagship franchise, it has something unique to offer that sets it apart just enough.

But obviously, where Lelu sets itself apart is in its presentation, which I think is probably the biggest reason it caught my attention in the first place. Rather than taking place in the sort of colorful, inviting fantasy world that Zelda fans have grown accustomed to, Lelu is almost entirely monochromatic, with its black-and-white environments giving the toy factory a rather unsettling atmosphere. It's an interesting contrast, especially considering that Lelu himself is a pretty adorable little character, and the idea of an innocent toy trying to escape a factory filled with other toys that want to kill him is a lot darker than the premise initially suggests. I wouldn't go so far as to call it a horror game, but there's definitely something eerie about the whole thing, and I think that works in its favor.

Lelu Has the Potential to Be More Than Another Zelda-Like

As much as I enjoyed my time with Lelu 's demo, I do wonder how well its formula will hold up once players have an entire game to explore, especially considering how much of the experience seems to revolve around navigating the same enormous toy factory. After all, part of what makes a game like Zelda so enjoyable is the variety of environments players get to visit, and while Lelu certainly has a distinct visual identity, there's always the possibility that its monochromatic presentation could start to feel a little repetitive after several hours. However, if the full game can continue introducing new abilities and increasingly elaborate puzzles while finding ways to make its different areas feel distinct from one another, I don't see why it couldn't become one of the more memorable Zelda -likes we've had in a while.

Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake's Greatest Upgrade Can't Be Seen
Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Refuses to Fix One Old Disappointment

And considering that Lelu is being developed by solo developer Jamie Rowan, I think what I've played so far is particularly impressive. There's clearly a lot of love for Zelda here, to the point that I couldn't help but laugh when Clocky asked me to find his missing Cuckoos, but I'm glad Rowan didn't stop at simply borrowing Nintendo's ideas and giving them a different coat of paint. The toy factory setting and its unsettling atmosphere give Lelu enough personality that I'm genuinely interested in seeing what else it has to offer when it launches on January 21, 2027. For now, though, I'd encourage anyone who enjoys Zelda -likes to give the free Steam demo a try, especially since it only takes about half an hour to see why this little clockwork toy has me so excited for what's next.

And considering that Lelu is being developed by solo developer Jamie Rowan, I think what I've played so far is particularly impressive. There's clearly a lot of love for Zelda here, to the point that I couldn't help but laugh when Clocky asked me to find his missing Cuckoos, but I'm glad Rowan didn't stop at simply borrowing Nintendo's ideas and giving them a different coat of paint. The toy factory setting and its unsettling atmosphere give Lelu enough personality that I'm genuinely interested in seeing what else it has to offer when it launches on January 21, 2027. For now, though, I'd encourage anyone who enjoys Zelda -likes to give the free Steam demo a try, especially since it only takes about half an hour to see why this little clockwork toy has me so excited for what's next.
